method: COMPILED FROM 3 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders' (vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012), 29 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 2.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC3488504 ('distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0)')). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Emory University MNT4P program, Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN) Management Guidelines Portal 'UCD Nutrition Management Guidelines, First Edition (v1.3)' (first edition April 2026, v1.3, updated April 2026), 12 claims; LICENCE: No licence or reproduction permission stated on the portal (disclaimer page read); treated as all rights reserved (read at https://managementguidelines.net/guidelines.php/152/disclaim/0/0/UCD and the portal footer). S3: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from British Inherited Metabolic Diseases Group (BIMDG) 'Hyperammonaemia: urea cycle disorders, OTC and CPS deficiencies (standard version), paediatric emergency protocol' (© BIMDG 2016, last reviewed May 2023), 4 claims; LICENCE: © BIMDG 2008/2016 (no licence or reproduction permission in the PDF or on bimdg.org.uk) (read at the PDF footer and the bimdg.org.uk site footer). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. The 2019 first revision (Häberle et al., J Inherit Metab Dis 42:1192–1230, doi:10.1002/jimd.12100) is closed access (Unpaywall: closed; Wiley returned 403) and could not be read, so this guideline uses the open 2012 original. Retried 2026-09-24: Unpaywall and OpenAlex still list it as closed, and the two repository copies (ZORA Zurich, Digital.CSIC) sit behind Anubis bot challenges, which were not bypassed. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the GMDI/SERN UCD Nutrition Management Guideline (first edition, April 2026; web pages fetched and tag-stripped, recommendation, detail and table pages concatenated), which draws on the 2019 revision, and S3, the BIMDG paediatric emergency protocol for OTC and CPS deficiency (PDF, pdftotext reading order; its dose table survived extraction). The S1 claims and fragments are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 3 (prenatal testing), Table 4 (actions by ammonia level), Table 5 (acute IV doses by disorder) and Table 8 (long-term oral doses). S1 Tables 1, 2, 6 and 7 have merged cells and were not extracted.

claims.claim: **UCDs can present acutely or chronically at any age,** often triggered by catabolism, a protein load or some drugs; symptoms are nonspecific (neurological, gastrointestinal, psychiatric). Take a detailed family history with pedigree.
claims.source_text: UCDs may present with acute or chronic presentations at any age and are often triggered by catabolic events, protein load or some drugs. In many cases a precipitating factor cannot be identified. Clinical signs and symptoms are nonspecific and commonly neurological, gastrointestinal or psychiatric. It is essential that healthcare professionals have an awareness of these diseases. Key questions should be asked and a detailed family history with pedigree is mandatory.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any unexplained encephalopathy or acute psychiatric illness, at any age, must prompt a plasma ammonia.** In a newborn with suspected sepsis, hyperammonaemia is always in the differential.
claims.source_text: UCDs must be included in the differential diagnosis of acute unexplained encephalopathy or acute psychiatric illness at any age, which must prompt plasma ammonia determination. … In newborns with clinical distress where sepsis is suspected, hyperammonemia must always form part of the initial differential diagnosis.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ammonia must be available as an emergency test, with results in 30 minutes.** Measure it for unexplained change in consciousness, unusual neurological illness, liver failure or suspected intoxication.
claims.source_text: Ammonia should be determined in an emergency setting with results available in 30 minutes. … Ammonia should be measured in patients of any age presenting 1) an unexplained change in consciousness; 2) unusual or unexplained neurological illness; 3) liver failure; 4) suspected intoxication.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If ammonia is high, start further metabolic tests immediately, without delaying treatment.** Genetic testing is the first-choice confirmation.
claims.source_text: If ammonia is found elevated, further metabolic investigations should be immediately carried out without delaying specific treatment. … Genetic testing is the method of first choice to confirm the diagnosis.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prenatal testing (S1 table, grade D):** mutation analysis on DNA from chorionic villi or amniotic fluid cells is listed for every disorder (chorionic villi only for arginase deficiency). Other options: enzyme assay on a late fetal liver biopsy in CPS1 and OTC deficiency (very limited experience); amniotic fluid citrulline in ASS deficiency, or argininosuccinate and its anhydrides in ASL deficiency; enzyme assay in chorionic villi or cultured amniotic cells in ASS, ASL and HHH; and fetal red-cell enzyme assay at mid-gestation in arginase deficiency. One mutation in a female OTC fetus cannot predict the phenotype (lyonisation). In NAGS deficiency, tell the woman first that lifelong treatment can fully normalise the phenotype.
claims.source_text: [Table 3] Prenatal testing of UCDs: Recommended analyses and sample requirements [Table 3 row 1] Disorder: NAGSD · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC a [Table 3 row 2] Disorder: CPS1D · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC [Table 3 row 3] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in late fetal liver biopsy b [Table 3 row 4] Disorder: OTCD · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC c [Table 3 row 5] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in late fetal liver biopsy b,d [Table 3 row 6] Disorder: ASSD · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC [Table 3 row 7] Recommended tests: Citrulline in amniotic fluid [Table 3 row 8] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in intact or cultured CVS or in cultured AFC [Table 3 row 9] Disorder: ASLD · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC [Table 3 row 10] Recommended tests: Argininosuccinate and its anhydrides in amniotic fluid [Table 3 row 11] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in intact or cultured CVS or cultured AFC [Table 3 row 12] Disorder: ARG1D · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS [Table 3 row 13] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in fetal blood erythrocytes (mid-gestation sampling) [Table 3 row 14] Disorder: HHH syndrome · Recommended tests: Mutation analysis using DNA from CVS or AFC [Table 3 row 15] Recommended tests: Enzyme assay in CVS or cultured AFC [Table 3 footnote] First choices are given in bold-type. CVS, chorionic villus sampling. AFC, amniotic fluid cells. Grade of recommendation, D . a The woman should be informed prior to prenatal testing that in NAGSD the phenotype can be normalized completely with life-long substitutive therapy. b Very limited experience (single patient report) and test not widely available. c The presence of one mutation in a female fetus cannot predict the phenotype given the effect of lyonization. d Informative in males but interpretation not clear in females due to lyonization-caused X-mosaicism.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay therapy.** Stop protein, start IV 10% glucose, give first-line medications, collect plasma and urine without postponing treatment, and transfer to a specialist centre.
claims.source_text: therapy must not be delayed. Pediatric hospitals should always have first-line medications and consensus-based written protocols on how to proceed. Patients in hyperammonemic crisis should be transferred without delay to a specialist centre after: … 1) stopping protein intake 2) starting intravenous (IV) 10% glucose … 4) plasma and urine collection for diagnostic purposes without postponing treatment initiation.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ammonia scavengers, L-arginine or L-citrulline (and carglumic acid in NAGS deficiency) are the key acute drugs;** watch for toxicity from repeated boluses or high doses of benzoate or phenylacetate. Carglumic acid may also be used in neonatal hyperammonaemia of unknown cause.
claims.source_text: Administration of ammonia scavengers, of L-arginine or L-citrulline and in NAGS deficiency, of carbamylglutamate, is highly valuable for treating acute hyperammonemic decompensation. The potential toxicity of repeated boluses or high doses of benzoate or phenylacetate should be taken into account. … may also be used as an emergency drug during acute neonatal hyperammonemia of unknown etiology.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Dialysis in children when ammonia exceeds 500 μmol/L or there is no response within four hours of medical treatment;** in adults, extracorporeal detoxification is first line. Haemodiafiltration is the method of choice; do not use exchange transfusion.
claims.source_text: In neonates and children with symptomatic hyperammonemia, dialysis should be carried out when ammonia exceeds 500 μmol/L or when there is no response within four hours after starting medical treatment. … Extracorporeal detoxification is the first line treatment in acute hyperammonemic decompensations in adults. … The method of choice for ammonia detoxification is hemodiafiltration. Peritoneal dialysis is a far less effective method. Exchange transfusion should not be used.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep the patient anabolic with high-dose glucose plus lipids** (once a fatty acid oxidation disorder is excluded). Reintroduce protein when ammonia is below 100 μmol/L, ideally within 24–48 hours.
claims.source_text: For treatment of acute hyperammonemia it is crucial to promote and maintain anabolism by infusing high-dose glucose plus lipids (if a fatty acid oxidation disorder has been excluded). Protein should be reintroduced when ammonia returns to <100 μmol/L. Ideally the period of protein-free nutrition should not exceed 24-48 hours.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prognosis is very poor** after more than 3 days of hyperammonaemic coma, clearly raised intracranial pressure, or a peak ammonia above 1000 μmol/L; weigh this before treatment.
claims.source_text: Before treatment of acute hyperammonemia, the prognosis and expected neurodevelopmental outcome must be considered since it can influence the therapeutic decision. Prognosis is considered very poor if: 1. hyperammonemic coma has lasted more than 3 days 2. intracranial pressure is clearly increased 3. ammonia peaked at >1000 μmol/L
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Baby at risk at birth (previous early-onset sibling):** within 30 min start 10% glucose at 4 ml/kg/h; after 4 symptom-free hours give protein-free feeds with oral sodium benzoate and L-arginine 50 mg/kg 6-hourly; check ammonia at 6 h.
claims.source_text: Within 30 min 10% glucose infusion (4 ml/kg/h) should be started and after 4 symptomless hours, protein-free feeds should be given, along with reduction of glucose infusion, and administration of PO 6-hourly 50 mg/kg of both sodium benzoate and L-arginine. Plasma ammonia should be measured at 6 h
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **GMDI: take protein away for no longer than 24 hours,** because prolonged restriction drives catabolism and negative nitrogen balance. Meanwhile give 100–125% of estimated energy from carbohydrate and fat: IV dextrose (for example a glucose infusion rate of 10 mg/kg/min in neonates), IV lipid at 1–3 g/kg/day, and oral or enteral feeds as early as they can be started. If glucose climbs (above about 150-200 mg/dL), add insulin so the dextrose can continue, checking glucose hourly while it runs.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Emory University MNT4P program, Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN) Management Guidelines Portal, 'UCD Nutrition Management Guidelines, First Edition (v1.3)', first edition April 2026, v1.3, updated April 2026, https://managementguidelines.net/guidelines.php/152/UCD, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Bring protein back in steps (GMDI):** restart after 24 hours without protein or once ammonia is below 100 μmol/L, whichever is first; begin at 25-50% of the target and add 25-50% a day as tolerated. An EAA-based medical food can be used first, alone or with intact protein, especially in severe neonatal presentations; in neonates, human milk can supply the protein. After dialysis, start higher, at 50-75% of the target.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Emory University MNT4P program, Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN) Management Guidelines Portal, 'UCD Nutrition Management Guidelines, First Edition (v1.3)', first edition April 2026, v1.3, updated April 2026, https://managementguidelines.net/guidelines.php/152/UCD, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **IV L-arginine hydrochloride (GMDI), except in arginase deficiency:** about 200-400 mg/kg in CIT-I (ASS deficiency) and ASA (ASL deficiency), then oral L-arginine; about 100-250 mg/kg in OTC and CPS deficiency, then oral L-citrulline.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Emory University MNT4P program, Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN) Management Guidelines Portal, 'UCD Nutrition Management Guidelines, First Edition (v1.3)', first edition April 2026, v1.3, updated April 2026, https://managementguidelines.net/guidelines.php/152/UCD, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Laboratory monitoring in a crisis (GMDI):** ammonia every 2-4 hours while treating, then every 3-12 hours while protein is reintroduced; plasma amino acids up to daily but not within 24 hours of a diet change; glucose and electrolytes often, glucose up to hourly on insulin.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Emory University MNT4P program, Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN) Management Guidelines Portal, 'UCD Nutrition Management Guidelines, First Edition (v1.3)', first edition April 2026, v1.3, updated April 2026, https://managementguidelines.net/guidelines.php/152/UCD, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Actions by ammonia level in a symptomatic patient (S1 table, grade C-D).** Above the upper limit of normal: stop protein (for 24 h, at most 48 h), give IV glucose to stop catabolism (10 mg/kg/min in a neonate) with insulin if needed, and check ammonia every 3 h. Above 100 (above 150 in neonates) and below 250 μmol/L: start IV L-arginine and nitrogen scavengers, and in an undiagnosed patient also carbamylglutamate, carnitine, vitamin B12 and biotin; in a known UCD, continue L-arginine (and continue or add L-citrulline in NAGS, CPS1 or OTC deficiency) with sodium benzoate, with or without phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate, at higher or IV doses, and consider nasogastric carbohydrate and lipid unless the child is vomiting.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Higher levels (S1 table):** at 250 to 500 μmol/L give every drug IV, prepare haemo(dia)filtration if encephalopathy is significant, ammonia was high early, or onset was on day 1 or 2, and begin it if ammonia does not fall rapidly within 3–6 h. At 500 to 1000, start haemo(dia)filtration immediately in the undiagnosed, and as fast as possible in a known UCD. Above 1000, weigh whether to continue curative treatment or move to palliative care.

claims.claim: **Cautions alongside (S1 table):** avoid exchange transfusion, hypotonic fluids and repeated drug boluses. High glucose is dangerous (hyperosmolarity); with high lactate (above 3 mmol/L), lower the glucose rate rather than add insulin, and check glucose 30 min after starting insulin and then hourly. Add sodium and potassium by the electrolytes, counting the sodium in the scavengers (7 mmol per gram of sodium benzoate, 5.4 mmol per gram of sodium phenylbutyrate). Never give L-arginine in arginase deficiency. Monitor phosphate and supplement early, especially with haemodialysis.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Acute IV doses for an undiagnosed patient (S1 consensus table, grade D; each in 10% glucose):** sodium benzoate 250 mg/kg over 90–120 min, then 250-500 mg/kg/d (5.5 g/m2/d above 20 kg); sodium phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate 250 mg/kg over 90–120 min, then 250-500 mg/kg/d; L-arginine hydrochloride 250(−400) mg/kg (1-2 mmol/kg) over 90–120 min, then 250 mg/kg/d; and N-carbamylglutamate (oral or enteral only) 100 mg/kg by nasogastric tube, then 25–62.5 mg/kg every 6 h. Consider also carnitine 100 mg/kg IV, hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM or IV and biotin 10 mg IV or orally.

claims.claim: **Scavenger rules (S1 table):** in severe decompensation give sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate together; in milder cases start with benzoate and add phenylbutyrate/phenylacetate if ammonia persists or rises. Adapt starting doses to ammonia and amino acids, and do not exceed 12 g a day of benzoate, phenylbutyrate or L-arginine. Arginine is usually unnecessary if citrulline is given. On haemodialysis or haemodiafiltration raise maintenance doses to 350 mg/kg/day.
claims.source_text: [Table 5 footnote] In severe acute decompensation both sodium benzoate and sodium PBA/phenylacetate should be given in parallel as " ultima ratio" . In less severe cases, a stepwise approach with initial sodium benzoate and if hyperammonemia persists or worsens, the addition of sodium PBA/phenylacetate can be chosen. The doses given can be used at the start of treatment but must be adapted depending on plasma ammonia and amino acids levels. Maximal daily dosages of sodium benzoate, sodium PBA and L-arginine should not exceed 12g for each of the three drugs. Grade of recommendation, D . a If citrulline is given, there is usually no need for concomitant use of L-arginine. … c If on hemodialysis/hemodiafiltration maintenance doses should be increased to 350mg/kg/day (or proportional increase for body surface-based dose calculation).

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start IV fluids at once if the child is unwell or vomiting:** a 20 ml/kg 0.9% saline bolus if circulation is poor or the child is shocked, then 10% glucose with 0.45% saline at 5ml/kg/h only until the deficit plus 24-hour maintenance has been calculated. With full-dose sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate use 10% glucose; if they are not at full dose use 10% glucose with 0.18% saline.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay the scavengers (BIMDG):** a loading dose over 90 minutes of sodium benzoate 250 mg/kg, sodium phenylbutyrate 250 mg/kg and arginine 150 mg/kg, then 250 mg/kg of each every 24 hours as a continuous infusion. The daily maximum is 500 mg/kg for benzoate and for phenylbutyrate, which carry 3.5 and 2.8 mmol/kg/d of sodium respectively. Discuss doses with the regional metabolic centre after the first treatment.

claims.claim: **Mild cases treated by mouth (BIMDG):** 2-hourly glucose-polymer emergency feeds day and night, by tube if not tolerated, for up to 24-36hours; raise the usual oral scavengers (sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate up to 500 mg/kg/day, arginine 150 mg/kg/day) and split them 2-hourly to limit vomiting.
claims.locator: British Inherited Metabolic Diseases Group (BIMDG), 'Hyperammonaemia: urea cycle disorders, OTC and CPS deficiencies (standard version), paediatric emergency protocol', © BIMDG 2016, last reviewed May 2023, https://bimdg.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/ER-UCD1-v4_972421_09092016.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Watch closely (BIMDG):** start insulin if glucose exceeds 8 mmol/l rather than cutting glucose; add potassium once urine flows (hypokalaemia is common); at any hint of encephalopathy do neurological observations at least hourly and give concentrated fluids through a central line to limit cerebral oedema; reassess and repeat gases, ammonia and electrolytes every 4-6 hours.

claims.claim: **Long-term care rests on:** low-protein diet, essential amino acid supplements, vitamins and minerals, nitrogen-scavenging drugs, an emergency regimen for illness, and liver transplantation for selected patients.
claims.source_text: · low protein diet · essential amino acids supplementation · vitamin and mineral supplementation · medications to increase waste nitrogen excretion · caring for special situations and provision of emergency regimen in intercurrent illnesses · liver transplantation for selected patients.

claims.claim: **Diet needs a specialist metabolic dietitian;** FAO/WHO/UNU figures guide protein and energy. When natural protein tolerance is too low, give 20-30% of total protein as essential amino acids (up to 50% in arginase deficiency), split over 3 or 4 meals.
claims.source_text: Dietary treatment is a cornerstone of therapy. This warrants the particular expertise of a specialist metabolic dietitian to finely balance nutritional requirements with metabolic stability. The FAO/WHO/UNU recommendations can be used to guide the protein and energy requirements. … A reasonable approach [] is to provide 20-30% of the total protein intake as EAA supplements, except in ARGD1, when supplements of EAA can, if necessary, be increased to 50% of total protein because of the severity of protein restriction (see below). EAA's should be given as an equally divided dose with 3 or 4 main meals to enhance utilisation and prevent nitrogen overload.

claims.claim: **Take oral sodium benzoate and sodium phenylbutyrate 4-times daily with meals and plenty of fluid** to avoid mucositis or gastritis. Give written drug sheets to parents, pharmacists and carers.
claims.source_text: To avoid mucositis or gastritis, oral sodium benzoate and sodium PBA (as granules, tablets, or undiluted liquid preparations) should be taken 4-times daily during meals with abundant fluids. … Written drug treatment sheets should be provided to parents, pharmacists and persons involved in patient care.

claims.source_text: Sodium PBA causes menstrual dysfunction/amenorrhea in ~25% of postpubertal females [], and can decrease appetite, disturb taste and cause disagreeable body odour. Also it may deplete BCAAs and increase the risk of endogenous protein catabolism

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Long-term oral doses (S1 table, grade C-D), split into three or four doses with meals.** NAGS deficiency: carbamylglutamate 10–100 mg/kg/d only. CPS1 and OTC deficiency: sodium benzoate up to 250 mg/kg/d (maximum 12 g/d); sodium phenylbutyrate up to 250 mg/kg/d below 20 kg or 5 g/m2/d above (maximum 12 g/day); L-arginine 100-200 mg/kg/d below 20 kg or 2.5-6 g/m2/d above (maximum 6 g/d); L-citrulline 100-200 mg/kg/d (maximum 6 g/d). ASS deficiency: both scavengers, with L-arginine 100-300 mg/kg/d below 20 kg or 2.5-6 g/m2/d above. ASL deficiency: benzoate and arginine, no phenylbutyrate. Arginase deficiency: both scavengers, no arginine. HHH syndrome: both scavengers, L-arginine 100-200 mg/kg/d (2.5-6 g/m2/d above 20 kg) and citrulline.

claims.claim: **Notes to the long-term doses (S1 table):** most of the group rated sodium phenylbutyrate second choice, added when benzoate alone is not enough; citrulline may be preferable to arginine, and then arginine is not needed. Monitor benzoate and phenylbutyrate levels and fasting plasma arginine (70–120 μmol/L) to adjust doses. Some patients need more: the FDA- and EMA-approved phenylbutyrate doses are 450-600 mg/kg/d under 20 kg and 9.9-13 g/m2/d above.
claims.source_text: b Sodium PBA was considered of second choice for long-term treatment by most guideline group members. It should be given together with sodium benzoate in patients in which benzoate alone is not enough. c Serum/plasma levels of benzoate/PBA and plasma levels of arginine (aim are fasting levels of 70-120 μmol/L) should be monitored to adjust dosages and in case of high or repeated doses. d In some patients higher doses are needed, according to expert advice. For PBA, FDA and EMA approved doses are 450-600mg/kg/d in children of <20kg, and, above 20 kg bw, 9.9-13 g/m 2 /d. e Citrulline may be preferable. When given no need for concomitant use of L-arginine.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start the emergency regimen without delay (even at home) when illness threatens hyperammonaemia;** call the metabolic unit if there is no prompt improvement. Vaccinate on the normal schedule; treat fever above 38°C.
claims.source_text: If there is an immediate risk of hyperammonemia as a consequence of an intercurrent illness or other event, the emergency regimen (Table 6) should be started without delay, even at home. … If there is no prompt improvement the metabolic unit should be contacted urgently … Vaccinations do not substantially increase the risk of decompensations and are recommended at the same schedule as for healthy children. If temperature exceeds 38°C antipyretic treatment should be started.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. claims.claim: **Elective surgery only when fully well, in a centre that can manage hyperammonaemia;** switch drugs to IV and infuse 10% glucose the day before.
claims.source_text: elective surgery should be undertaken when the patient is completely well including no minor intercurrent illness and has normal ammonia/amino acid levels. Surgery should only be carried out in centres prepared for dealing with acute hyperammonemic decompensations. The day before surgery drug treatment should be switched to IV and glucose (10%) infused to ensure anabolism.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. claims.claim: **Liver transplantation is the only cure;** ideally before irreversible neurological damage, generally between 3 and 12 months of age, for severe neonatal onset (not NAGS deficiency), progressive liver disease, recurrent crises despite treatment, or poor quality of life.
claims.source_text: The only available curative treatment for UCDs is liver transplantation, allowing return to a normal diet and stopping drug administration. … Liver transplantation should ideally be carried out before irreversible neurological damage and/or repeated crises, generally between 3 and 12 months of age. It may be considered in all patients (excepting NAGSD) with severe neonatal onset. It is also indicated for patients with progressive liver disease (e.g. ASLD), for those suffering recurrent metabolic decompensations and hospitalisations despite medical therapy, as well as those with poor quality of life.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. claims.claim: **Home plan for mild illness (GMDI):** cut protein by up to 50% for 24-48 hours, raise non-protein energy by at least 10-20% and fluids by 10-20%, and keep giving amino acid supplements and scavengers. Give the family warning signs, when to call the metabolic team, and an emergency letter; avoid long fasts and drugs that can precipitate a crisis, such as corticosteroids and valproate.

claims.claim: **Planned procedures (GMDI):** book the patient first on the list and admit the day before; keep the fast as short as is safe with continuous IV dextrose throughout; avoid long religious or exercise-related fasts.
